title: Risk Foundations
lessons/rk-1/steps/0/body: A **stop loss** is an order that closes your trade automatically if the price moves against you. That way, your loss never gets bigger than the amount you picked in advance.
lessons/rk-1/steps/0/tip: Golden rule: never enter a trade without a stop loss.
lessons/rk-1/steps/1/body: A **take profit** is an order that automatically **closes your trade in profit** when the price reaches your target. That way, greed can't make you give back the profit you've earned.
lessons/rk-1/steps/2/statement: A stop loss helps keep a trade's loss from growing past a set amount.
lessons/rk-1/steps/2/explanation: A stop loss closes the trade at the price you set in advance. (Only in very wild swings might there be a little slippage.)
lessons/rk-1/steps/3/prompt: You bought Bitcoin at $60,000 and set your stop loss at $58,800. What's the most you can lose per Bitcoin?
lessons/rk-1/steps/3/explanation: 60,000 − 58,800 = $1,200. Your loss can't get bigger than that.
lessons/rk-1/steps/4/sentence: Before you enter a trade, set your ___ so that if the price goes against you, your ___ stays limited.
lessons/rk-1/steps/4/explanation: A stop loss means deciding in advance the most you're willing to lose.
lessons/rk-1/steps/5/prompt: Where does the stop loss go on a buy trade?
lessons/rk-1/steps/5/explanation: In a buy, you lose money when the price falls, so the stop loss goes below the entry price.
lessons/rk-1/steps/6/prompt: You bought at the blue line (1.0850). Drag the red stop loss line down and place it just below the last swing low.
lessons/rk-1/steps/6/explanation: The last low is at 1.0822, so a sensible stop loss sits a few pips below it (say 1.0815). If the price breaks that low, your buy idea is no longer valid. Above the low, a normal swing would knock you out; much lower, and your loss grows for no reason.
lessons/rk-2/steps/0/body: **Risk** is the distance from your entry to your stop loss, and **reward** is the distance from your entry to your take profit. If the risk is 20 and the reward is 60, the ratio is **1:3**: for every $1 you risk, you could make $3.
lessons/rk-2/steps/1/body: With a **1:2** ratio, even if only **40%** of your trades win, you come out ahead overall. You don't have to be right all the time; you just need **small losses and big wins**.
lessons/rk-2/steps/2/prompt: Your stop loss is $20 from your entry and your take profit is $60 away. What's your risk-to-reward ratio?
lessons/rk-2/steps/2/explanation: 60 ÷ 20 = 3: for every 1 unit of risk, you're aiming for 3 units of profit. That's 1:3.
lessons/rk-2/steps/3/statement: To make money, more than half of your trades have to be winners.
lessons/rk-2/steps/3/explanation: With a good risk-to-reward ratio (say 1:2), you're profitable even with a 40% win rate.
lessons/rk-2/steps/4/prompt: Which trade has the better risk-to-reward ratio?
lessons/rk-2/steps/4/explanation: Risking 50 for a profit of 150 is 1:3, the best ratio of the options.
lessons/rk-2/steps/5/prompt: The entry (60,000) and stop loss (59,400) are set. Place the green take profit line where the risk-to-reward ratio becomes 1:2.
lessons/rk-2/steps/5/explanation: Risk = 60,000 − 59,400 = $600. For 1:2, the reward has to be 2 × 600 = $1,200, so the take profit goes around 61,200. That target is still below the previous high (around 61,650), so it closes before reaching that resistance.
lessons/rk-2/steps/6/sentence: If your risk is $10 and your reward is $30, your risk-to-reward ratio is ___ to ___.
lessons/rk-3/steps/0/body: Pros risk only **1 to 2 percent** of their whole account on each trade. With a $1,000 account, that's a loss of **$10 to $20** per trade at most. That way, a few losses in a row can't wipe out your account.
lessons/rk-3/steps/0/example/result/valu: 90% of the account is still intact
lessons/rk-3/steps/1/body: **Position size = risk amount ÷ stop loss distance.** Say you want to risk $20 and your stop loss is $2 below your entry. Your size is 20 ÷ 2 = **10 units**.
lessons/rk-3/steps/1/tip: Set your risk first, then work out the size; never the other way around.
lessons/rk-3/steps/2/prompt: Your account is $5,000 and you want to risk 1%. What's the most you can lose on each trade?
lessons/rk-3/steps/3/prompt: You want to risk $30 and your stop loss is $3 from your entry. How many units is your position?
lessons/rk-3/steps/3/explanation: 30 ÷ 3 = 10 units. If the stop loss gets hit, you lose exactly $30.
lessons/rk-3/steps/4/statement: After a loss, it's smart to double the size of your next trade to win it back.
lessons/rk-3/steps/4/explanation: Doubling your size after a loss (martingale) can empty your account very fast. The risk on each trade should stay the same.
lessons/rk-3/steps/5/pairs/0/meaning: Distance from entry to stop loss
lessons/rk-3/steps/5/pairs/1/meaning: Distance from entry to take profit
lessons/rk-3/steps/5/pairs/3/meaning: Risk amount divided by stop loss distance
